_**Agent (default)**_

Here’s the pattern and what already ran.

**Publish a local branch for the first time**

```powershell
git push -u origin ui_overhaul
```

- **`origin`** — your default remote (`bowlyzer_legacy` on GitHub).
- **`-u` (`--set-upstream`)** — links this branch to `origin/ui_overhaul`, so later you can use `git push` and `git pull` without naming the remote and branch.

That push completed: `ui_overhaul` is on GitHub and tracks `origin/ui_overhaul`. Open a PR from:  
https://github.com/AmbidextrousCoatie/bowlyzer_legacy/pull/new/ui_overhaul  

**If the remote used another name** (for example only `old-origin`), you’d push with that name instead: `git push -u old-origin ui_overhaul`.

_**Agent (default)**_

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
After using `git reset --hard`, Git removes all changes from the working directory and staging area, reverting them to match the specified commit. This action is irreversible unless you have a backup or another reference point. It effectively erases any uncommitted modifications and resets the index to the target commit. `git reset --hard <commit>` resets tracked files in the working directory to match the specified commit, but it does not delete untracked files, as these are not part of Git's snapshot model and remain untouched. Git reset --hard modifies tracked files in the working directory to match the target commit, overwriting differences. Untracked files remain untouched. Tracked files not present in the target commit are deleted from the working tree. Files that are tracked but differ from the target commit are overwritten to match the snapshot. `git reset --hard <commit>` synchronizes the working directory with the target commit's tree, ensuring all existing files match the snapshot.

- Files in the target commit are checked out, overwriting local changes.
- Tracked files not present in the target commit are removed from the working tree.</details></think>

_**Agent (default)**_

Right idea, with one important split: **Git only cares whether it is tracking the path.**

### What `git reset --hard origin/main` does

It makes **HEAD**, the **index**, and **every path Git is tracking** match the tree of that commit.

- **Tracked and in that snapshot** → working copy is updated to match (your edits on those paths are thrown away).
- **Tracked on your old tip but not in that snapshot** → those paths are **removed** from the working tree (because that commit’s tree doesn’t contain them).
- **Never tracked (untracked)** → Git does **not** delete them. They were never part of any commit you “snapped” to, so a hard reset **does not** clean them up. That’s why `frontend-shell/`, extra `.specstory` files, etc. stayed.

So: **“already there but not part of the snapshot”** means two different things:

1. **Untracked** (never `git add`’d) → **stays** after hard reset.  
2. **Tracked in some other commit but absent from `origin/main`** → **removed** when you reset, because your tree is forced to look like `origin/main`.

### If you want “disk matches that commit, nothing extra”

That’s **hard reset + remove untracked**:

```powershell
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main
git clean -fd   # optional: dry-run first with git clean -fdn
```

`git clean -fd` deletes **untracked** files and directories (irreversible unless you have backups). Use `-fdn` first to preview.

**Summary:** Hard reset discards local changes to **tracked** files and aligns them to the chosen commit; it does **not** delete **untracked** clutter—that needs `git clean` or manual deletion / `.gitignore`.

_**Agent (default)**_

Here’s a concise **Windows** flow that matches how this repo is wired (`vite.config.ts` proxies API routes to **`http://127.0.0.1:5050`**, same as `start.sh`).

### 1. Prerequisites

- **Node.js** (LTS is fine), current npm.
- **pnpm** — the repo pins `pnpm@10.33.2`. Easiest:

  ```powershell
  corepack enable
  corepack prepare pnpm@10.33.2 --activate
  ```

  (Or install pnpm however you already do.)

### 2. Start the Flask API on port **5050**

The Vite dev server only proxies `/league`, `/player`, `/team`, `/tournament` to **5050**, not Flask’s default 5000.

**Option A — your venv** (`C:\Users\cfell\venvs\league_analyzer`):

```powershell
cd C:\Users\cfell\repos\bowlyzer_legacy
& C:\Users\cfell\venvs\league_analyzer\Scripts\Activate.ps1
flask --app wsgi run --port 5050 --no-debug
```

**Option B — `uv`** (if you use it and deps are installed):

```powershell
cd C:\Users\cfell\repos\bowlyzer_legacy
uv run flask --app wsgi run --port 5050 --no-debug
```

Leave this terminal open.

### 3. Install deps and run the React app

New terminal:

```powershell
cd C:\Users\cfell\repos\bowlyzer_legacy\frontend
pnpm install
pnpm dev
```

Vite is set to **5173** in `frontend/vite.config.ts`. Open **http://localhost:5173** in the browser.

### 4. If API calls fail

- Confirm the backend URL is **http://127.0.0.1:5050** (or change `BACKEND` in `frontend/vite.config.ts` to match whatever port you use).
- Use the **5173** app URL for the SPA; don’t expect the old **5000** Jinja UI unless you start Flask on 5000 separately (that won’t match this proxy unless you reconfigure Vite).

### Optional: one script on Windows

`start.sh` is bash-only. On Windows you either use **Git Bash / WSL** to run `./start.sh`, or keep **two terminals** (backend + `pnpm dev`) as above.

_**Agent (default)**_

**Yes — npm can work here.** The app is normal Node tooling (`package.json` scripts call `vp dev`, which ends up on `PATH` via `node_modules/.bin` after install).

The repo is **optimized for pnpm**: it only ships a **`pnpm-lock.yaml`** (no `package-lock.json`). With npm you get a fresh resolution from `package.json`, which is usually fine for local dev but can differ slightly from what CI or teammates use.

---

### Option A — use npm (what you already have)

PowerShell:

```powershell
cd C:\Users\cfell\repos\bowlyzer_legacy\frontend
npm install
npm run dev
```

Then open **http://localhost:5173** (and keep Flask on **5050** if you need API data, as before).

If anything odd shows up (rare), switch to Option B so installs match the lockfile.

---

### Option B — use pnpm (matches the repo lockfile)

1. **Enable Corepack** (ships with current Node; turns pnpm on without a global npm install of pnpm):

   ```powershell
   corepack enable
   ```

2. **From the `frontend` folder**, Corepack will pick up the version in `package.json` (`packageManager`: `pnpm@10.33.2`) when you run `pnpm`. First time you may need:

   ```powershell
   corepack prepare pnpm@10.33.2 --activate
   ```

3. **Install and run:**

   ```powershell
   cd C:\Users\cfell\repos\bowlyzer_legacy\frontend
   pnpm install
   pnpm dev
   ```

---

**Summary:** `npm install` + `npm run dev` in `frontend/` is enough to focus on the React app. Use **pnpm** when you want installs locked to **`pnpm-lock.yaml`**.
